question_en: Shreya Bhatt, CFA, is an independent financial advisor who wants to grow her client base. At a dinner with several prospective clients, she states, "The knowledge and skills I have gained in the CFA program have enhanced my abilities in portfolio management. The rigor and intensity of the exams have trained me to work hard for my clients. As a CFA charterholder, I am best qualified to manage your money. My results speak for themselves. My clients have achieved an annualized rate of return of 10% over the past ten years, compared with 6% for my benchmark." Assuming her return figures are accurate, has Bhatt violated Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program?
option_b: No, since her statements are backed by facts.
option_c: No, since her statements were made verbally.
explanation_en: "Investment transactions for clients and employers must have priority over investment transactions in which a Member or Candidate is the beneficial owner." Standard VI(B) requires Members and Candidates to put clients' interests ahead of their own. This means clients should be financially unharmed by a Member's personal trades. To comply with the Standard, for a given security, client trades should be placed before nonclient (eg, employee) trades. If employees trade the same security before clients, employees may negatively impact the security's price (eg, higher prices for buys, lower prices for sells) for clients. The Standard allows Members and Candidate to make personal trades if they: Do not harm clients from their trades Do not receive an economic benefit from client trades Adhere to governing laws and regulations Even if the action contradicts previous investment recommendations (ie, selling after recommending a buy), investment professionals may invest according to their personal needs. Ashton Griffiths publicly makes a recommendation, promptly makes purchases for clients, and sells after receiving preclearance. He does not violate the Standard by selling Allthrift since clients are not harmed, he does not benefit from client trades, and he fulfills his regulatory obligations (Choices B and C).

question_en: Rashid Miah, CFA, negotiates with his employer, Tenor Capital, to work only part-time as a financial advisor while finishing a graduate degree, with the understanding that he will return to full-time work after graduation. After graduating, Miah remains employed part-time since Tenor does not have enough clients, and keeps him at a part-time status until more clients are obtained. Miah looks for ways to increase his income and arranges to advise friends and family on investment decisions for a fee when not working for Tenor. He also plans to work as a driver for a ridesharing company on weekends, when Tenor is closed. To comply with Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Agreements, Miah should obtain written permission from Tenor before pursuing:
option_b: both the investment advisory and the ridesharing.
option_c: neither the investment advisory nor the ridesharing.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information." Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information prohibits Members and Candidates from trading on or recommending investments based on material nonpublic information. However, analysts may piece together public and nonmaterial nonpublic data from multiple sources to form an investment conclusion. This research approach is referred to as the mosaic theory, and it recognizes that analysts form conclusions from various sources of information. Conclusions formed through the mosaic process, even when based on information that would be considered material and nonpublic if it were coming directly from a reliable source (eg, the company), do not violate the Standard. In this scenario, Lena Schmidt has used public information (eg, financial statements) and nonmaterial nonpublic information (ie, the CEO's flight) to form an investment conclusion using the mosaic approach. Although Schmidt's conclusion, if true, would be the equivalent of material nonpublic information if disclosed directly to her by the company, her actions do not violate the Standard. (Choice B) A CEO's travel plan is typically deemed a nonmaterial event (ie, by itself, it would not affect the company's stock price). Therefore, Schmidt did not need to wait for the company to issue a press release to make the information public. (Choice C) Analysts are not required to publicly disseminate their research reports. As long as Schmidt's report was sent to clients in a fair manner, she has not violated the Standard.

question_en: Tim Green, CFA, is an investment advisor for Steady Hand Advisors (SHA). While attending a charity function, Green runs into one of his clients, Dr. Walter Kowalski. Kowalski tells Green about a small-cap biotechnology company developing a new process that could be a medical breakthrough. Green says he is familiar with the company but considers its stock to be very speculative since the company has never been profitable or even produced a viable product. Nevertheless, Kowalski instructs Green to buy 10,000 shares of the stock when the market opens the next day. Green advises against the trade: although an investment of this size will have an immaterial impact on Kowalski's portfolio, it does not meet his investment objectives and violates the constraints of his investment policy statement (IPS). Still, Kowalski insists that Green execute the trade. The next morning, Green documents his rationale for why the trade is unsuitable on SHA's unsolicited trade request form. Green emails the form to Kowalski to sign and return so the trade can be executed at the market open. Do Green's actions comply with Standard III(C) Suitability?
option_b: No, the investment is unsuitable regardless of portfolio impact.
option_c: No, since Green is required update the investment policy statement.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that anyone subject to their supervision or authority complies with applicable laws, rules, regulations, and the Code and Standards." Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors requires Members and Candidates who supervise employees to make a reasonable effort to detect and prevent unethical behavior and violations of the law, rules established by their firm, and the Code and Standards. However, failing to detect such behavior is not necessarily a violation of the Standard if the supervisor ensures that a proper compliance system is in place. The Guidance to the Standard indicates that compliance, at a minimum, requires supervisors to: establish written compliance procedures, and perform regular reviews to ensure that employees are following the procedures. A supervisor who does not satisfy these requirements violates the Standard even if no laws or codes were violated. However, the concept of "reasonableness" does not make supervisors responsible for detecting all violations; employees may be able to evade compliance in ways that cannot be detected through reasonable efforts. In this instance, Ross Farley established and implemented an adequate compliance program (Choice B). It is not reasonable to conclude that Farley should have known that an employee would try to evade the requirement (Choice C). However, now that he knows it is possible, Farley should enhance the compliance systems to prevent future occurrences.

question_en: Chen Hong, CFA, is an independent investment advisor. Through a referral from an existing client, Chen contacts Zhao Qiuping. Chen briefly meets with Zhao, who is leaving for vacation the next day. Zhao agrees to be Chen's client and sends him money that is currently in her savings account. They are not able to discuss the details of Zhao's financial circumstances and objectives at the meeting, but Zhao tells Chen that he can invest the money however he sees fit and agrees that they will meet again to create a detailed investment policy statement when Zhao returns. Chen invests a portion of Zhao's funds in several stocks of companies that Chen has invested in other clients' funds, since Chen believes the stock prices will increase and Chen does not want Zhao to miss out. By the time Zhao returns, her investment portfolio is up 4%. With regards to Zhao's investments, Chen:
option_a: was in full compliance with the Standards.
option_b: violated the Standards by not getting approval from Zhao for each investment.
option_c: violated the Standards by investing Zhao's funds before gathering appropriate information.
explanation_en: "When referring to CFA Institute, CFA Institute membership, the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program, Members and Candidates must not misrepresent or exaggerate the meaning or implications of membership in CFA Institute, holding the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program." Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program forbids Members and Candidates from exaggerating the meaning or implication of having a CFA charter. This includes overstating competency or the ability to achieve superior investment performance. Although Standard I(C) focuses generally on promises related to investment guarantees or ability to achieve superior returns, Standard VII(B) specifies that these claims cannot be attributable to the CFA designation. However, statements of objective fact about the benefits (eg, knowledge and skills gained, credibility) of the CFA designation and the rigor of the program are allowed. In this question, Gamal's first statement violates the Standard by asserting that Osiris Partners is an elite asset management firm since the firm hires only CFA charterholders; by doing so, she attributes elite status to the charter. Even though the statement compares the firm's performance against the market, the statement is still a violation since it implies superior performance can be expected going forward. Gamal's second statement does not violate the Standard since it states only facts about the intensity of the exam and skills and knowledge earned (Choices B and C).

question_en: Archer Clegg, CFA, manages a fund of illiquid distressed real estate that primarily consists of properties located in economically depressed areas. Clegg does not report fund performance relative to a benchmark since there are no benchmarks based on distressed real estate. Clegg uses two reputable appraisal firms to value each property annually. Last year, a new appraisal firm was hired due to cost and timing concerns involving a previous appraiser. Since then, Clegg has noticed that the new firm appears to consistently undervalue properties compared with the other firm doing appraisals. Fund performance reports are prepared using the average of the two appraisals, a method that is disclosed to clients and potential clients. Has Clegg most likely violated Standard I(C) Misrepresentation?
option_b: Yes, since he is not using only the lowest appraisal.
option_c: Yes, since he fails to compare performance to a benchmark.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must disclose to their employer, clients, and prospective clients, as appropriate, any compensation, consideration, or benefit received from or paid to others for the recommendation of products or services." Standard VI(C) Referral Fees requires Members and Candidates to notify their employers, existing clients, and prospective clients of any benefit they receive for recommending a product or service. Disclosing referral arrangements allows employers and clients to determine if conflicts of interest exist and whether a recommendation is impartial. A referral fee is broadly defined and includes any cash or noncash rewards. In this question, Trevor Collins violates the Standard for both referrals since the Standard stipulates that all referral agreements must be disclosed. The referral for life insurance must be disclosed to clients since the referral fee can cause a conflict of interest for Collins whether it comes from an internal or external source (Choice B). The referral for advanced tax services must be disclosed to clients with full details so clients can make informed judgments; it is not enough to simply disclose the existence of an agreement (Choice A).

question_en: Bo Shun Zheng, CFA, is a journalist who writes articles on market sentiment for a major news organization. She uses various sources, including social media, analyst interviews, and more conventionally published research. In one article, she reproduces research published on social media by an analyst known only as "Big Alpha." Since she does not know Big Alpha's real name, she includes the research without citation, noting only that it has been endorsed by "a leading investment expert." Regarding Standard I(C) Misrepresentation, does Zheng most likely violate the Standard?
option_a: Yes, by not citing the source of the research.
option_b: Yes, by using research available only on social media.
option_c: No, because she protects Big Alpha's choice to hide his true identity.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information." Standard II(A) requires Members and Candidates to abstain from investment actions if they have material nonpublic information (MNI). Trading based on MNI erodes trust in the fairness of the capital markets and the investing profession by perpetuating the idea that insiders take deceitful advantage of the investing public. MNI can come from many sources, including company management and expert networks. A Member or Candidate must evaluate the information itself to decide whether it is MNI before acting on it. In this question, the physician whom Sumit Ahuja calls through an expert network provides information on broad industry trends, which is nonmaterial since it is not company specific. The physician also provides the names of companies with drugs in the final stages of the government approval process, which is public information. Therefore, Ahuja did not receive MNI through the expert network and did not violate the Standard by acting on it (Choice B). Although research reports from sell-side analysts, even those based on opinions, can be material and nonpublic, trading based on these reports does not violate the Standard if any investor can purchase them. Such availability means that a report is public even if not publicly disseminated. Since the report Ahuja purchased from Vijaya Dayal is available to all investors, Ahuja did not violate the Standard by acting on it (Choice C).

question_en: Christine Hansen, CFA, works as an investment advisor at a large regional bank. Many of Hansen's larger clients can benefit from comprehensive estate planning, including the need for various trusts and insurance policies. For the trust work, Hansen refers these clients to an outside law firm, and for their insurance needs, she refers them to the bank's internal insurance subsidiary. Hansen receives a one-time $100 bonus for every insurance policy sold by the subsidiary on her referral. The law firm is a corporate sponsor of the local professional basketball team and gives Hansen two courtside tickets for each referral. With regard to Standard VI(C) Referral Fees, Hansen is required to disclose:
option_b: only the internal referral arrangement.
option_c: only the external referral arrangement.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must make full and fair disclosure of all matters that could reasonably be expected to impair their independence and objectivity or interfere with respective duties to their clients, prospective clients, and employer. Members and Candidates must ensure that such disclosures are prominent, are delivered in plain language, and communicate the relevant information effectively." Members and Candidates who serve as directors have a conflict of interest between serving their employer's clients and the board's shareholders. The existence of a conflict alone does not necessarily violate the Standard. If an employee receives stock compensation as a director, the employee must: Disclose the compensation to the employer Disassociate from the investment decisions regarding the external company Since Miles McAllen's directorship is approved by Everhold Securities and McAllen discloses his compensation, McAllen does not violate the Standard (Choices A and B). Firms that allow employees to maintain directorships at external public companies must prevent them from making investment judgments on those companies since conflicts of interest exist. Therefore, McAllen must not participate in analyzing or giving opinions about 4Furniture, Inc. to abide by the Standard. A suggested solution is for firms to establish a firewall to mitigate the conflict.

question_en: Jalen Butler, CFA, is a research analyst for Principal Capital. As part of his research, Butler uses aggregated data generated from a variety of social media websites to track trends. Principal's compliance department updates its record retention policies annually, and therefore its most recent rules do not include several of the new websites used by Butler. Butler does not retain the data generated from the websites outside of Principal's record retention list since the information is on the internet and therefore is easily accessible. Has Butler most likely violated the Standards?
option_b: No, since certain sources are not on Principal's record retention list
option_c: No, since he is not required to retain records of information that can be found on the internet
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in any professional conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, or deceit or commit any act that reflects adversely on their professional reputation, integrity, or competence." Members and Candidates must comply with Standard I(D) by abstaining from behaviors that diminish the individual's, firm's, or investment industry's reputation. Deceitful or dishonest acts negatively impact a Member's or Candidate's integrity and violate the Standard. In this scenario, if Juniper Securities does not pay equitable wages to all employees, the matter should be pursued through the appropriate channels while maintaining compliance with the Standard. Emilia Cosgrove violates the Standard by falsifying her travel expenses to Juniper regardless of her subjective belief that doing so is warranted. Cosgrove diminishes her reputation and the reputation of the investment industry by dishonestly reporting her expenses (Choice A). (Choice C) Cosgrove and Manuel Griggs may share personal information, including how much they earn, without violating the Standard.

question_en: Liu Tengfei, CFA, manages a set of client portfolios. Several of his portfolios are underperforming for the quarter. Liu's boss tells him that Golden Peak, a pharmaceutical company, has a drug that is expected to receive regulatory approval soon, and the approval is likely to increase the price of the stock. After analyzing Golden Peak's financials, Liu purchases Golden Peak stock for only his underperforming portfolios. Two weeks later, the drug receives regulatory approval and the stock increases 35%. Has Liu most likely violated Standard III(C) Suitability?
option_b: No, since Golden Peak's stock increased in value
option_c: No, since he allocated Golden Peak to only underperforming client portfolios
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates have a duty of loyalty to their clients and must act with reasonable care and exercise prudent judgment. Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their clients and place their clients' interests before their employer's or their own interests." A client practices directed brokerage by directing brokerage commissions for the purchase of goods or services that aid the beneficiaries of the client's account. This practice is common among plan sponsors who outsource the responsibility of day-to-day investment decisions to subadvisors and do not directly generate commissions themselves. Trading commissions are considered an asset of the client—in this scenario, State Pension Fund (SPF), represented by Juan Castillo—not the subadvisor. The client has the right to make beneficial use of that asset, and the subadvisor has a duty of loyalty to use the asset for the benefit of the client if so requested. Castillo, on behalf of SPF (ie, the client), instructs several subadvisors to direct trade commissions (ie, the asset) to Johnson Brothers Brokerage to pay for Macro Trade Research Advisors' research services. Castillo complies with Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care by using directed brokerage to pay for investment research related directly to SPF's investment decisions and to SPF's benefit. (Choices B and C) Castillo does not misuse his position or violate his duty of loyalty to the pension fund. Since trading commissions are assets of the client, it is appropriate to sometimes request that those assets be used to acquire research services (ie, direct subadvisor trades) for the benefit of the client (ie, the pension plan).

question_en: Kyle Trainor, CFA, publishes a popular investing newsletter. In the most recent edition he recommends that subscribers buy Ambit Holdings (AHC). Trainor has owned AHC for many years and would like to sell it, but he believes that AHC is undervalued at its current price of $25 per share. His recommendation is based on interviews with AHC's executives as well as his own independent research, and he believes that AHC's price will double when it releases its year-end earnings next month. He includes a few details of his research, using phrases such as "I have heard that earnings will be very strong" and "Many people think that this stock will SOAR." He also discloses his ownership of AHC stock. Based on his recommendation, many subscribers buy AHC stock, which causes the price to rise. Before AHC releases its year-end earnings, Trainor sells his entire AHC position at a price of $45 per share. After AHC releases its earnings report, its price continues to rise, peaking at $64 per share before declining. Did Trainor most likely violate Standard II(B) Market Manipulation?
option_b: Yes, since his recommendation was premised on opinion, not fact.
option_c: Yes, since he benefitted from the price increase caused by his recommendation.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information." Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information prohibits Members and Candidates from acting on or causing others to act on information that is both material and nonpublic. The Standard applies only if both elements are present. Information is nonpublic if it is not available to the investing public in general. In this scenario, Western Aerospace initially provides no information about the contract except to confirm that it is negotiating with the government. It does not announce that the negotiations failed until after Duane Wolfe sent his email. Therefore, prior to the announcement, information concerning the contract's status, including what Wolfe overheard, is nonpublic. Information is material if: a reasonable investor would consider it important to know before making an investment decision or the information would likely impact the stock price. With respect to materiality, information's reliability must be considered. Wolfe cannot assess the veracity of what he overheard since he does not know the speakers. In addition, his source at Western Aerospace cannot confirm what he overheard. Therefore, the overheard conversation is unreliable, rendering the information immaterial (Choice A). Although Wolfe may have violated Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis by sending his email, he did not violate Standard II(A). (Choice C) Given Wolfe's stature as an analyst, it is reasonable to conclude that his email caused clients to act. Had the email been based on material nonpublic information, Wolfe would have violated Standard II(A).

question_en: Ashton Griffiths, CFA, a world-renowned investor, is an adviser at TenSteps Investments. On a popular podcast, Griffiths publicly recommends purchasing shares of Allthrift, a large online bank. At Griffiths' direction, TenSteps has held Allthrift for over 7 years for clients and Griffiths is still confident that it is an excellent investment. The next day, TenSteps buys 100,000 shares for clients. After the trade, Allthrift price declines 2%. Two weeks later, after receiving preclearance, Griffiths sells 10,000 shares of Allthrift from his private account for tax purposes and to purchase a second home. According to Standard VI(B) Priority of Transaction, does Griffith most likely violate the Standard?
option_b: Yes, by purchasing Allthrift for clients.
option_c: Yes, by selling Allthrift after recommending its purchase.
explanation_en: "Investment transactions for clients and employers must have priority over investment transactions in which a Member or Candidate is the beneficial owner." Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions requires members and candidates to place clients' and employers' financial interests before their own when conducting investment transactions. It is not uncommon for a member or candidate to transact in the same investments as clients, or even alongside clients. A Member or Candidate does not violate the Standard provided that: the client is not disadvantaged by the trade, the member or candidate does not benefit from the client transactions, and the member or candidate adheres to all applicable regulatory requirements. In this scenario, Pappas complied with the Standard. (Choice B) Blackout periods are specifically intended to prevent "front-running," which is placing personal trades or a firm's proprietary trades ahead of client trades. In this instance, by combining and executing all trades at once, Pappas is investing alongside her clients, as she has previously communicated. Therefore, a blackout period is not applicable given the circumstances. (Choice C) In this case, the client was not disadvantaged nor did Pappas benefit from the client transactions; therefore, Pappas did not violate the Standard by executing her trades alongside her clients' trades.

question_en: Ross Farley, CFA, is the chief compliance officer at Prudent Advisors, Inc. (PA). PA offers investment advisory services to retail investors. Farley monitors the activity of six financial advisors to ensure compliance with all applicable laws and regulations. Farley has provided all employees with the firm's code of ethics and a policies and procedures manual. On an annual basis, Farley conducts educational training, sets expectations for behavior, and asks employees to sign a document attesting that they have received the code and manual and understand their contents. In addition, employees are required to submit a quarterly transaction report detailing their trading of individual securities. Farley discovers that Greg Smith, an advisor at the firm, recently opened an unauthorized account at a discount brokerage firm and is conducting personal trades that have not been reported or approved. According to Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors, did Farley most likely violate the Standards?
option_b: Yes, for failing to set up and implement an effective compliance program
option_c: Yes, for failing to prevent Smith from trading in an unauthorized brokerage account
explanation_en: "When referring to CFA Institute, CFA Institute membership, the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program, Members and Candidates must not misrepresent or exaggerate the meaning or implications of membership in CFA Institute, holding the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program." Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program regulates how Members and Candidates may use the CFA designation. Candidates are those who have: registered with CFA Institute and are enrolled to sit for an exam, or sat for an exam and are awaiting results. Since Anisa Bhandari has received her results but has not registered for the next scheduled exam, she is no longer considered an active Candidate (Choice A). When Bhandari successfully registers for Level II, she can consider herself a Candidate again. (Choice C) Candidates may disclose their prior participation in the CFA program or may factually state that they passed a certain exam. Language such as "Passed Level I of the CFA Program" is acceptable.

question_en: Reem Gamal, CFA, is the owner of Osiris Partners. She is working on the marketing pitch that she will give to the trustees of Horus University to have Osiris manage its endowment fund. As part of her pitch, she plans to say: I: "Since Osiris hires only CFA charterholders, we are among the elite asset management firms, as proven by our performance: Our returns have outperformed the overall market in 9 of the past 10 years." II: "By passing such an intense and comprehensive study program, each of our analysts have enhanced their knowledge in portfolio management, including endowments." Which of the statements would most likely violate the Standards?
option_b: Only Statement II
option_c: Both Statement I and II
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must make full and fair disclosure of all matters that could reasonably be expected to impair their independence and objectivity or interfere with respective duties to their clients, prospective clients, and employer. Members and Candidates must ensure that such disclosures are prominent, are delivered in plain language, and communicate the relevant information." Personal ownership of stock recommended or held in client portfolios is a common potential conflict of interest that requires disclosure. Here, Warner appropriately disclosed his ownership of HRE stock to his employer. However, Standard VI(A) also requires disclosure of his personal ownership of HRE stock to clients and prospective clients. This is meant to allow clients to decide for themselves whether the potential conflict of interest might influence a candidate's or member's objectivity (Choice B). (Choice C) That Warner held the stock and did not sell it for a gain is not relevant to the requirement to disclose his personal holding in the published report.

question_en: Trevor Collins, CFA, is a financial adviser for Starlight Advisory. Some of his clients require additional services outside his expertise. Collins refers clients who need life insurance to another department at Starlight. The life insurance department gives Collins 10% of each client's initial life insurance payment as a referral fee. Collins does not disclose this arrangement to clients since the referral is internal to his company. Collins refers clients who need advanced tax services to Accounting Hub, a third-party accounting firm. For every 10 referrals, Accounting Hub invites Collins to join the firm's managers in their corporate box for a professional football game. Collins discloses to clients that he has a referral agreement with Accounting Hub but does not disclose the details. Collins most likely violated the Standards with respect to:
option_a: only the internal life insurance referral.
option_b: only the third-party advanced tax services referral.
option_c: both the internal life insurance and third-party advanced tax services referrals.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information." Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information prohibits Members and Candidates from acting on or recommending investments based on material nonpublic information. However, analysts may piece together public and nonmaterial nonpublic data from multiple sources to form an investment conclusion. This process is referred to as mosaic theory. Recommendations based on mosaic theory do not violate the Standard since, rather than rely on company insiders, the conclusions depend on the analyst's skill in synthesizing information from disparate sources. In this scenario, the researcher reiterates the company's already publicly released statement on the prospects and timeline for commercial development of a new battery technology, so no nonpublic information was disclosed. The researcher's comments regarding rare earth elements being in short supply might provide some additional nonmaterial information since it can be reasonably assumed that the information is included in the company's publicly released forecasts or otherwise publicly available. Therefore, Maya Levine did not violate the Standard since she disclosed no material nonpublic information. Levine used this information in applying mosaic theory to assist with the investment thesis for the rare earth mining company (Choice B). (Choice C) Although it is recommended that Members and Candidates report the receipt of potentially material nonpublic information to their supervisor or compliance staff, it is not required in all circumstances, and Members and Candidates are urged to exercise their own judgment, as appropriate.

question_en: Sumit Ahuja, CFA, is an investor with limited knowledge of the biotech industry. Through an expert network, he calls a physician at a prestigious hospital regarding broad trends in the biotech industry. The physician names several companies that have high-profile drugs in the final stages of the government's publicly disclosed approval process. One of the companies is Orion Pharmaceuticals. After the call, as part of his thorough research on Orion, Ahuja purchases a newly released research report from Vijaya Dayal, a respected biotech analyst who covers Orion. In her report, Dayal states that Orion's drug is likely to receive regulatory approval, based on her own opinion from thorough research. As a result, Ahuja purchases stock in Orion. Ahuja:
option_a: was in full compliance of the Standards.
option_b: violated the Standards by trading based on information received from the expert network.
option_c: violated the Standards by trading based on a research report that was not disseminated to
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must use reasonable care and judgment to achieve and maintain independence and objectivity in their professional activities. Members and Candidates must not offer, solicit, or accept any gift, benefit, compensation, or consideration that reasonably could be expected to compromise their own or another's independence and objectivity." Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity requires Members and Candidates to avoid actions that compromise their independence and objectivity or create conflicts of interest. Producing issuer-paid research is an acceptable practice as long as the analyst conducts the research with due diligence, remains independent, and discloses all conflicts. One way to maintain independence is to accept only a flat fee for this type of work, since a variable fee linked to conclusions, recommendations, or outcomes could inhibit the analyst's independence and objectivity. In this scenario, Landry and O'Connor both violated the Standard by agreeing to tie compensation to outcomes (ie, new investors). (Choices B and C) Novogratz did not violate the Standard by proposing his distribution arrangement since this compensation is not based on any specific outcome and cannot be seen as compromising his independence.

question_en: Miles McAllen, CFA, is a research analyst for Everhold Securities. For the last several years, McAllen has analyzed 4Furniture, Inc. for Everhold. McAllen joins 4Furniture's board of directors and receives 500 shares of 4Furniture's common stock as compensation, which is disclosed to and approved by Everhold. According to Standard VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts, does McAllen's directorship most likely violate the Standard?
option_a: Yes, since McAllen's objectivity is compromised.
option_b: Yes, as McAllen must refuse external compensation.
option_c: No, but McAllen may not make investment decisions on 4Furniture.
explanation_en: Members and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information." Standard II(A) requires Members and Candidates to abstain from taking investment actions based on material nonpublic information (MNI) related to a security. Buying and selling of the security may occur only after the information is publicly disclosed. Members and Candidates who trade using MNI might generate short-term profits, but their actions diminish the integrity of capital markets and the investment profession over the long term. In this scenario, Nadine Pinot violates the Standard by basing her recommendation on MNI. The new technology improvements could reasonably be expected to move the company's stock price, making the information material. The information also has not been publicly disclosed by the company (Choices B and C). Pinot must evaluate her interaction with Pierre Johann and determine whether it provided her with MNI. Pinot should conclude that the information she received is material, and since it has not been publicly disclosed, she should not use it in her recommendation.

question_en: Emilia Cosgrove, CFA, is considering a job offer to work as an analyst for Juniper Securities. It is the only offer she has received after five months of searching for employment. Manuel Griggs, Cosgrove's close friend, was hired by Juniper six months ago and currently works there as an analyst. In confidence, Cosgrove shares her offer with Griggs, who in turn shares his salary. Griggs is paid 30% more than the salary offered to Cosgrove. Cosgrove negotiates for higher compensation, but Juniper stands by its original offer. She accepts the offer and begins working for Juniper. Whenever she travels on assignments for Juniper, she requests reimbursement for amounts that exceed her actual expenses. According to Standard I(D) Misconduct, do Griggs and/or Cosgrove most likely violate the Standard?
option_b: Yes, Cosgrove violates the Standard by compromising her integrity.
option_c: Yes, Cosgrove and Griggs violate the Standard by sharing salary information.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must use reasonable care and judgment to achieve and maintain independence and objectivity in their professional activities. Members and Candidates must not offer, solicit, or accept any gift, benefit, compensation, or consideration that reasonably could be expected to compromise their own or another's independence and objectivity." Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity requires Members and Candidates to refuse any compensation that could reasonably be expected to compromise their independence and objectivity. Sell-side analysts can be compensated by companies for writing research reports about the company. However, analysts must be careful not let the compensation affect their judgement. The report must reflect an independent opinion following diligent and thorough research. Compensation from the company should not be linked to the conclusion of the report. Forms of compensation that violate that Standard are those that can reasonably be expected to bias the analyst's opinion directly (eg, payments based on the rating) or indirectly (eg, stock options, warrants). Best practice calls for a flat fee paid by the company. Analysts are required to disclose the compensation in their report, including the nature of the compensation, but disclosure does not offset a violation of accepting influential compensation (Choice C). (Choice B) Although the report reflected Huang's independent opinion, this opinion can be reasonably viewed as biased by clients due to the nature of the compensation (ie, stock options) for writing the report, thus violating he Standard.

question_en: Juan Castillo, CFA, is director of research at State Pension Fund (SPF). SPF invests exclusively through subadvisors to construct the pension's portfolio. While preparing for SPF's annual strategy session, Castillo contacts Macro Trade Research Advisors (MTRA) to get its latest research and views on the financial markets. MTRA has a correspondent brokerage relationship with Johnson Brothers Brokerage (JBB) in which JBB directs 50% of commissions to MTRA. Castillo instructs several subadvisors to send trades to JBB to pay for MTRA's research services. Do Castillo's actions most likely comply with Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care?
option_b: No, since Castillo cannot direct other firms' trades.
option_c: No, since Castillo uses pension fund assets to pay for research services.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must: Exercise diligence, independence, and thoroughness in analyzing investments, making investment recommendations, and taking investment actions. Have a reasonable and adequate basis, supported by appropriate research and investigation, for any investment analysis, recommendation, or action." Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis states that Members and Candidates must perform reasonable and standardized due diligence on external advisers. In addition to reviewing an adviser's investment process, strategy, performance presentation, and internal controls, Members and Candidates must review the adviser's code of ethics. In this scenario, Enes Yilmaz conducts thorough due diligence and confirms that the hedge fund operates in compliance with local laws, as required by the Standard. However, he also discovers that the company does not have an established code of ethics. Without a code of ethics, Yilmaz cannot be confident that the firm will adhere to a high level of ethical standards. Therefore, by investing with this manager, Yilmaz violates Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis. (Choice B) Given the circumstances, the hedge fund is not required to conform to the Standards. However, before investing, Yilmaz must ensure a minimum level of internal controls and decision-making protocols, including an established code of ethics. (Choice C) Yilmaz has a fiduciary duty to the pension plan participants but also must adhere to the higher ethical standards imposed on CFA charterholders.

question_en: Duane Wolfe, CFA, is a well-regarded equities analyst. Advisors in his firm routinely forward his reports and other communications to their clients. Wolfe covers a company called Western Aerospace, a major military contractor. Western Aerospace is rumored to be close to signing a significant government contract and based on the rumors its stock price has steadily increased. The company confirms only that contract talks are ongoing. Many clients of Wolfe's firm own Western Aerospace stock. At a restaurant after work, Wolfe overhears two individuals he does not know talking about Western Aerospace's contract negotiations and implying that the deal will fall through. Wolfe immediately calls a source at Western Aerospace, but the source neither confirms nor denies what Wolfe overheard. The next morning, Wolfe sends an email to the firm's client advisors that says, "Heads up: I may have information that could significantly affect Western Aerospace's stock price." He provides no further details. Several client advisors forward the email to their clients, many of whom interpret it to mean that the contract will not happen and therefore sell their stock. Later that day, Western Aerospace announces that there will be no government contract, and its stock price declines significantly. Has Wolfe most likely violated Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information?
option_b: No, since the information Wolfe overheard was unreliable.
option_c: No, since Wolfe did not know that his email would cause clients to sell their stock.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in any professional conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, or deceit or commit any act that reflects adversely on their professional reputation, integrity, or competence" Under Standard I(D) Misconduct, Members and Candidates must refrain from conduct that diminishes the integrity, reputation, or competence of the industry, a firm, or themselves. Although the CFA Institute recommends that Members and Candidates always act responsibly, the Standard focuses on how a Member's behavior impacts professional activities. The integrity of the profession is founded on the belief that Members and Candidates act in a trustworthy manner; otherwise, the industry's overall reputation is diminished. In this scenario, to violate the Standard, Eugene Power must be intoxicated while working in a professional capacity. He does not violate the Standard by being intoxicated and making personal trades. The location of his work is irrelevant, but the nature of the work matters. By itself, intoxication is not a violation of the Standard, but carrying out professional duties—such as interviewing potential clients or writing an investment policy statement while intoxicated—calls into question Power's judgment and competence and violates the Standard (Choices A and C).
